summary: Supply the initial height, the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal position and the Projectile motion experiment calculator solves for initial velocity (V). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Projectile motion experiment calculator work?
sections.html:
The Projectile motion experiment calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports initial velocity (V) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the initial height (h), the time of flight (t), the maximum height (hmax) and the horizontal position.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Projectile motion experiment calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Initial velocity (V)=initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) ÷ the cosine of (angle of launch (α))
Angle of launch (α)=(initial vertical velocity (Vy) ÷ initial velocity (V))
Gravitational acceleration=2 × (initial height (h) + time of flight (t) × initial vertical velocity (Vy)) ÷ (time of flight (t) ^ 2)
Distance (d)=time of flight (t) × horizontal velocity
Gravitational acceleration=-(initial vertical velocity (Vy) ^ 2) ÷ (2 × initial height (h) − 2 × maximum height (hmax))
Initial velocity (V)=the square root of ((initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) ^ 2) + (initial vertical velocity (Vy) ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) = 10 m/s, Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg and Gravitational acceleration = 9.8067 m/s². The calculator returns Initial velocity (V) = 10.154266 m/s, Initial vertical velocity (Vy) = 1.763 m/s and Horizontal velocity = 10 m/s.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Initial velocity (V) = 10.154266 m/s, Initial vertical velocity (Vy) = 1.763 m/s and Horizontal velocity = 10 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Initial horizontal velocity (Vₓ) = 10 m/s and Angle of launch (α) = 10 deg.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Projectile motion experiment calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial height, the time of flight and the maximum height — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Projectile motion experiment calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns initial velocity (V), derived from the initial height, the time of flight and the maximum height. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Projectile motion experiment calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial height, the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal position, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial velocity (V) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial velocity (V) opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Initial velocity (V) = 10.154266 m/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Projectile motion experiment calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
